records.name: Poland
records.summary:
Poland is broadly workable with two genuinely traveler-relevant weaknesses and a low-but-improving social baseline. In detention, Poland has documented severe failures involving foreign trans people directly: a Vietnamese trans woman was held in a male immigration-detention center with her hormone-therapy needs ignored, and the European Court of Human Rights found Poland violated a trans prisoner's rights by denying her HRT (2024). There is no specialized trans prison section analogous to Italy's Rebibbia.

Socially, the climate was deeply hostile under the previous Law and Justice government ("LGBT-free zones") and is improving under the Tusk coalition (a hate-speech reform draft in March 2025; ceased investigating foreign same-sex marriages), but a low baseline persists — Pride marches have been violently attacked (Białystok 2019), online anti-LGBT harassment is documented (Amnesty 2025), and rural areas draw harassment warnings. Legal gender recognition is court-based and medically gatekept, with no self-ID.

Bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute. Major cities are calmer than rural areas.

sources.claim: Association for Legal Intervention (SIP) news (March 2024): a transgender Vietnamese citizen was placed by a Polish regional court in a guarded centre for male foreigners despite identifying as a woman and undergoing hormone therapy since 2018 (stopping would be detrimental); SIP secured her release - documenting detention-placement problems for trans migrants in Poland.

TGEU (July 2024): the ECtHR ruled Polish prison authorities violated a trans woman's Article 8 rights by denying her access to hormone replacement therapy in prison (EUR 8,000 damages) - strengthening trans prisoners' right to life-saving treatment.

Amnesty International report (Sept 2025) 'A Thousand Cuts': technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X - quantitative experiment and content labelling documenting targeted online abuse.
HRW World Report 2025 Poland chapter: the Tusk coalition government began addressing rule-of-law concerns from the PiS era; includes a Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Poland: new hate-speech law plans (January) expanding protections to gender identity and sexual orientation; a second bill (October) notably omitted gender identity as a protected category; a mayor was sentenced for a homophobic letter to the PM; legislative flux on hate-crime protections.
Government of Canada travel advice for Poland (updated Aug 2026): 'Take normal security precautions'. General travel advice, not trans-specific.

Polish legal journal article (Przegląd Sejmowy, 2024, in Polish) by Podgórska-Rykała and Kępa: 'Current Legal and Administrative Situation of Transgender Persons in Poland. Selected Issues' - analyses the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act and their impact on trans people's status, equality and protection.

Human Rights Watch (Mar 2007): 'Poland: School Censorship Proposal Threatens Basic Rights' — warns the proposed penal-code amendment would criminalise virtually all school discussion of homosexuality, targeting LGBT education and anti-discrimination work.

records.name: Puerto Rico
records.summary:
A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.

sources.claim: Advocates for Trans Equality 'Know Your Rights' guide to US airport security (TSA): body-scanner flags, pat-downs, documentation mismatches, and how to request alternative screening - relevant to Puerto Rico as a US territory under TSA procedures.

Human Rights Watch (Mar 2026): 'US State Revokes Gender-Affirming Identification' — Kansas voids birth certificates and driver's licenses not matching sex assigned at birth; US document-policy context relevant to US territories.
Washington Blade (April 2019): Puerto Rico activists criticized religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills moving through the island's legislature.
Washington Blade (June 2014): four same-sex couples joined the Puerto Rico marriage lawsuit challenging the island's marriage ban.
Washington Blade (March 2019): Puerto Rico lawmakers blocked a vote on a bill to ban conversion therapy for minors.
Washington Blade (June 2019): Puerto Rico's governor told lawmakers to withdraw the religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills - a win for LGBT advocates on the island.

Erin in the Morning (July 2025): Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalizes the provision of gender-affirming hormone treatment or surgery for anyone under 21, even with consenting parents. This can include 15 years in prison, a $50,000 fine, and the loss of any medical certifications; potentially even parents could be charged. Civil-rights groups said they would challenge the ban in court. The governor positioned themselves as LGBTQ-friendly during the election, but proved harshly anti-trans while in office.

records.name: North Korea
records.summary: North Korea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code — but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad provisions on obscene activities give authorities unlimited discretion; reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. The concept of gender identity simply does not exist in public life (BBC Korea: sexual minorities are “denied as a concept”). Tourists are under constant escort and surveillance; any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention in the world's most totalitarian system.

sources.claim: Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): no laws appear to penalise consensual same-sex acts in the 1950/2009 Criminal Code, but Article 193 prohibits 'decadent culture' (including sexual video recordings) and Article 262 prohibits collective 'obscene activities'; the state denied the existence of same-sex activity in 2014; an unconfirmed 2011 report claimed execution of a lesbian couple; no freedom of assembly.

LegalClarity overview (May 2026): North Korea has no law explicitly criminalising same-sex activity, but broad provisions on 'decadent culture' and 'obscene activities' give authorities wide discretion; the government publicly denies LGBT people exist; defectors describe deeply repressive reality.

BBC Korean (Oct 2024, in Korean): 'Does same-sex love exist in North Korea?' - feature on the near-total erasure of North Korean sexual minorities; interviews with defector writer Jang Young-jin; notes new laws (Pyongyang Cultural Language Protection Act, Youth Education Guarantee Law, Rejection of Reactionary Thought and Culture Law) further tightening control; the state does not even acknowledge the concept.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - the totalitarian regime's pervasive abuses; the report notes no specific law criminalising same-sex conduct but the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

US State Department 2020 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - no reliable information on LGBT persons; the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant human-rights reality.
CNN (Apr 2017): 'I could not even dream: Life as a gay North Korean' — a defector's account of homosexuality's place in North Korean society and its punishment.

KCNA commentary (April 2014): the North Korean state news agency's attack on Michael Kirby, chair of the UN Commission of Inquiry - calling him 'a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality' and claiming homosexuality 'can never be found in the DPRK boasting of sound mentality and good morals' - an official statement of the regime's homophobia.

records.name: Portugal
records.summary:
Portugal remains one of the world's safest destinations for transgender visitors. The 2018 self-determination law allows legal gender and name change without medical requirements (minors 16-17 with parental consent), bathroom access matching one's gender is legally protected, conversion therapy is banned (2024), intersex infant surgery is banned, and hate-crime law covers gender identity — within an EU rule-of-law environment with very low violent crime. Same-sex marriage since 2010.

Two caveats pull it just below its Iberian neighbour Spain. First, in March 2026 the Portuguese parliament approved in first reading three bills (backed by the governing PSD/CDS and the far-right Chega) that would repeal the 2018 self-ID law, reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion, and ban hormones for minors. As of the most recent reporting this is not yet final law — it is in committee, and a government technical opinion warned it may be unconstitutional — so the self-ID framework is still in force. Second, hate-crime reports rose about 38% in both 2023 and 2024, with acknowledged under-reporting.

For a visitor these translate to a real political-hostility signal and elevated but still low-level harassment risk, not criminal exposure. The practical day-to-day environment is calm and welcoming, particularly in Lisbon and Porto.

sources.claim: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026 (May 2026): Spain tops the ranking of 49 countries; the map and index document LGBTI human-rights laws and policies across Europe, with commentary on the gap between legal progress and daily experience.
Público (March 2026, in Portuguese): the Portuguese Parliament (AR) approved PSD, Chega and CDS bills reversing the gender-identity law - first vote to roll back self-ID legal gender recognition.

Observador (March 2026, in Portuguese): the right revokes the gender-identity regime - what may change and what each bill provides; PSD, CDS and Chega voted to reverse the regime allowing gender change without medical validation; hormones for minors would be banned.

Joint statement (March 2026) by IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal calling on the Portuguese Parliament to reject three bills attacking trans and intersex rights - a serious attack on rights, dignity, safety and bodily autonomy that would drop Portugal at least 4 places on the Rainbow Map.

Forbidden Colours (March 2026): condemns the approval in general terms of three anti-trans bills (151-79), backed by Chega and governing PSD/CDS-PP; the bills target the self-identification law (Law 38/2018), would reintroduce medical gatekeeping, and one Chega bill bans discussing LGBTIQ+ topics in schools (mirroring Hungary/Russia 'anti-propaganda' laws).

KET Magazine (March 2026): Portugal set to roll back its trans self-determination law - the first-reading vote would reintroduce a mandatory medical opinion for legal gender/name change, undoing the 2018 reform (self-declaration from 16); human-rights groups warn of medicalised gatekeeping, delays, costs and arbitrary refusals.

TVI/Lusa (April 2026, in Portuguese): the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality (CIG) confirms in a technical analysis that the current gender-identity law is aligned with international standards and that self-determination is protected by the Portuguese Constitution; the Chega bill 'rests on discontinued terminology' and non-consensual definitions.

The Portugal Brief (Aug 2026): legal gender changes edge back toward their 2024 record (606 in 2024, 541 in 2025; ~3,300 total since 2018), concentrated in Lisbon, as Parliament moves to reimpose the medical test the 2018 self-determination law scrapped.

European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 (2026), 'Health and safety of transgender people in Portugal' — an MEP questions the Commission on the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its health-and-safety impact on trans people.
OSCE/ODIHR page on Portugal's hate-crime legislation (Decree Law 48/95, amended by Law 15/2024): excerpts including Article 132 aggravated murder with SOGI-related aggravating circumstances.

Equaldex data for Portugal: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support for same-sex parenting (ranked #1 of 30 EU regions).

Portuguese Ombudsman: requests a review of the constitutionality of Article 176-C of the Penal Code, which establishes the crime of acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression - an unusual challenge to a protective provision.

records.name: Paraguay
records.summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors — South America's most conservative country. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ Paraguayans feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, Asunción has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.

sources.claim: AP (Sep 2025): 'For Paraguay's transgender women, survival often means leaving home' — discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of hometowns into migration and sex work.

Amnesty International Paraguay report 2025: criminalization of human rights defenders and structural discrimination persisted; high levels of gender-based violence; threats against journalists and repression of social protest.

Amnesty International, State of the World's Human Rights - Paraguay 2024: rulings on 10 lawsuits regarding legal recognition of transgender people's names were still pending; a new bill and parliamentary commission of inquiry threatened civil-society freedom of association and expression; gender-based violence a huge concern.

PinkNews (Oct 2017): Paraguay's Ministry of Education banned public schools from using materials on 'gender ideology'; Education Minister Enrique Riera said he would 'burn books' spreading it; LGBT organisations called 'gender ideology' a phrase 'invented by conservative groups to keep justifying violence and discrimination'; Amnesty also condemned the move.

Tico Times (Jan 2018): the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled that all signatory countries must allow same-sex marriage - binding for most Latin American states including Paraguay; ~300 Costa Ricans celebrated at the court.
ABC Color (in Spanish): 'Gays pueden adoptar niños' - Paraguayan media coverage of gay adoption (page largely navigation content at fetch time).

Última Hora (Jan 2018, in Spanish): international human-rights expert Claudio Nash said Paraguay must adapt its laws for equal marriage per the IACHR recommendation - the Inter-American Court could oblige Paraguay to change its norms, and the country should start discussing implementation rather than wait for a judgment.

records.name: Palestinian Territories
records.summary: The Palestinian Territories are dangerous for trans visitors, with a hard internal split. In the West Bank, same-sex conduct is not criminalised (1951 Jordanian code) but there are no protections, family/clan hostility is severe, and LGBT Palestinians flee to Israel for safety (Israeli courts now grant such asylum claims). In Gaza, a British Mandate law technically allows 10 years, Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality, and the territory is in a catastrophic war. Cairo 52 notes trans identities are not explicitly criminalised but gender-affirming healthcare is essentially destroyed/unavailable.

sources.claim: Cairo 52 country review of the Palestinian Territories: Gaza and the West Bank have distinct penal codes; trans identities not explicitly criminalised in either; homosexuality laws seldom enforced; gender-affirming healthcare severely limited (destruction of hospitals in Gaza, occupation); no clear legal gender recognition due to multiple jurisdictions; Israel's portrayal as a safe haven for LGBTQ+ Palestinians criticised as pinkwashing.

LegalClarity overview (June 2026): no unified legal code - the West Bank (Jordanian Penal Code 1960) does not criminalise same-sex conduct, while Gaza retains a British colonial-era law punishing it with up to 10 years; neither territory offers anti-discrimination protections, relationship recognition or a gender-transition pathway; social and family-level persecution poses risks independent of statute.

Wikipedia overview: mixed legality - West Bank legal since 1951 with equal age of consent; Gaza unclear; sections on civil rights and violence, health, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict (including alleged blackmailing by the Israeli military), and LGBTQ activism (Aswat).

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - covers Palestinian territories, including the work of al-Qaws and the legal situation under both Palestinian Authority and Hamas governance.

Times of Israel: rights groups slammed Palestinian police for banning LGBTQ activity - after the police action against al-Qaws, the foundation received a wave of hate messages which activists said 'pose a serious threat' to the gay community.

HRW + Women's Centre for Legal Aid and Counselling + Equality Now joint statement (June 2018): on Palestinian women's rights and legal protections - context for the broader rights environment in the Palestinian territories.

Times of Israel: Israel to allow LGBT Palestinians granted temporary asylum to work - some 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.

records.name: French Polynesia
records.summary:
French equality law applies in full — gender-identity anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions since 2017, a conversion-practice ban since 2022, and legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites — and it lands on genuinely entrenched indigenous ground: the mahuu third-gender role predates colonisation, rae-rae identities are visible in daily life across the archipelago, the territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023 with government and church participation, and travel literature calls the openness cultural rather than legal.

The undertow is real but social, not statutory: the rights overview records varying stigma, employment discrimination, and episodic transphobic violence that has pushed some rae-rae into sex work, while healthcare depth thins sharply outside the main island. For a visitor the combination is among the region's strongest — law, culture, and visibility aligned — with the standard framework caveat that the state's prison-system findings apply here too, and small-island anonymity cuts both ways.

sources.claim: BuzzFeed News feature (Jan 2018, French context): trans women in France incarcerated on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal gray area - relevant to French Polynesia as a French overseas collectivity applying French law.

CGLPL opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty (French context, applicable in French Polynesia): serious violations persist across places of detention.

Grokipedia page on transgender rights in Tahiti: French anti-discrimination law applies (gender-identity protections since 2012, hate crimes since 2017, conversion-therapy ban since 2022); legal gender recognition without restrictions; culturally, the māhū third-gender role predates colonisation, while modern rae-rae identities face varying stigma; transphobic violence and employment discrimination pushing some rae-rae into sex work persist.

OutTraveler (April 2025): 'French Polynesia doesn't need Pride flags to earn its place on every LGBTQ+ bucket list' - openness is 'ingrained in the culture'; the māhū (traditional third gender) and rae-rae are visible in daily life; 118 islands with direct flights from major cities.

RNZ Pacific (Dec 2023): French Polynesia held its first international colloquium on LGBTQIA+ rights ('Our voices, our rights, our Pacific Way') at the University of French Polynesia - with government, church and regional participants; recalled that the third gender (Rae-rae in French Polynesia, Faʻafafine in Samoa) is a well-entrenched, accepted part of Polynesian society.
Out Adventures gay travel guide for French Polynesia: 'a relaxed, gay-welcoming South Pacific culture' across Tahiti and Bora Bora's 118 islands - travel-oriented assessment of the destination.

records.name: Qatar
records.summary:
Qatar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf. Human Rights Watch interviewed four transgender women arrested by the Preventive Security Department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Arrests continued even during the 2022 World Cup under international scrutiny.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (Oct 2022): 'Qatar: Security Forces Arrest, Abuse LGBT People' — arbitrary arrests, abuse and preventive-detention practices against LGBT people, including ahead of the 2022 World Cup.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex acts illegal since 1938 (Sharia may be applied), penalty up to 7 years (de jure death penalty, unenforced); no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no relationship recognition; covers the 2022 FIFA World Cup controversy and living conditions.

PinkNews (July 2018): Theresa May urged to advocate for LGBT people in Qatar during the Emir's London visit - Qatar is one of 74 countries punishing same-sex relations with imprisonment; attention focused on its record ahead of the 2022 World Cup.
